# Direction Angle of a 2D Vector in Terms of Arctangent

## Statement

Let $\mathbf a$ be a vector quantity embedded in a Cartesian plane $P$, expressed in component form as
$$\mathbf a = x\,\mathbf i + y\,\mathbf j ,\qquad x,y\in\mathbb R ,$$
where $\mathbf i,\mathbf j$ are the unit vectors in the positive directions of the $x$- and $y$-axes. Let $\theta$ denote the direction of $\mathbf a$, measured from the positive direction of the $x$-axis and normalised to lie in the half-open interval $(-\pi,\pi]$. Then
$$\theta=\begin{cases}
\arctan\dfrac yx & x>0,\\[4pt]
\arctan\dfrac yx+\pi & x<0 \text{ and } y\ge 0,\\[4pt]
\arctan\dfrac yx-\pi & x<0 \text{ and } y< 0,\\[4pt]
\dfrac\pi2 & x=0 \text{ and } y>0,\\[4pt]
-\dfrac\pi2 & x=0 \text{ and } y<0,\\[4pt]
\text{undefined} & x=0 \text{ and } y=0,
\end{cases}$$
where $\arctan$ denotes the real arctangent, i.e. the inverse of the restriction of $\tan$ to $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$.

The claim is true as stated; we prove it.

## Conventions and facts used

**(D) Definition of direction.** The magnitude of $\mathbf a = x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j$ is $r=\lVert\mathbf a\rVert=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$. If $\mathbf a\ne\mathbf 0$ then $r>0$, and the *direction* of $\mathbf a$ is the angle $\theta$, measured from the positive $x$-axis, determined by
$$\mathbf a=r\bigl(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+\sin\theta\,\mathbf j\bigr),
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\cos\theta=\frac xr,\quad \sin\theta=\frac yr, \tag{1}$$
the angle being normalised to lie in $(-\pi,\pi]$. The zero vector has no direction. From now on, until Case 6, we assume $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$, so that $r>0$.

**(E) Existence and uniqueness of $\theta$.** *For every pair $(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2$ with $u^2+v^2=1$ there is exactly one $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta=u$ and $\sin\theta=v$.*

*Proof.* **Existence.** Since $u^2+v^2=1$ we have $u\in[-1,1]$. The cosine function is continuous and strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos 0=1$ and $\cos\pi=-1$; hence by the Intermediate Value Theorem there exists $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\alpha=u$ (and it is unique in $[0,\pi]$ by strict monotonicity). Then $\sin^2\alpha=1-u^2=v^2$, and $\sin\alpha\ge 0$ on $[0,\pi]$, so $\sin\alpha=\lvert v\rvert$.

*If $v\ge 0$:* put $\theta=\alpha\in[0,\pi]\subseteq(-\pi,\pi]$. Then $\cos\theta=u$ and $\sin\theta=\lvert v\rvert=v$.

*If $v<0$:* then $\sin\alpha=\lvert v\rvert>0$, so $\alpha\in(0,\pi)$; put $\theta=-\alpha\in(-\pi,0)\subseteq(-\pi,\pi]$. Then $\cos\theta=\cos\alpha=u$ (cosine is even) and $\sin\theta=-\sin\alpha=-\lvert v\rvert=v$ (sine is odd).

**Uniqueness.** Suppose $\theta_1,\theta_2\in(-\pi,\pi]$ both satisfy $\cos\theta_i=u$, $\sin\theta_i=v$. By the cosine difference formula,
$$\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)=\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2+\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2=u^2+v^2=1 ,$$
so $\theta_1-\theta_2\in 2\pi\mathbb Z$. But $\theta_1,\theta_2\in(-\pi,\pi]$ forces $\lvert\theta_1-\theta_2\rvert<2\pi$, whence $\theta_1-\theta_2=0$. $\square$

Applying (E) to $(u,v)=(x/r,\,y/r)$ — which satisfies $u^2+v^2=(x^2+y^2)/r^2=1$ — shows that for $\mathbf a\ne\mathbf 0$ the direction $\theta$ exists and is *uniquely* determined by (1). This is what makes the case analysis below legitimate: in each case we pin $\theta$ down from (1) alone.

**(S) Signs of $\cos$ and $\sin$ on $(-\pi,\pi]$.** For $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$:

* $\cos\theta>0\iff\theta\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$;
* $\cos\theta=0\iff\theta\in\left\{-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right\}$;
* $\cos\theta<0\iff\theta\in\left(-\pi,-\frac\pi2\right)\cup\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right]$;
* $\sin\theta>0\iff\theta\in(0,\pi)$;
* $\sin\theta=0\iff\theta\in\{0,\pi\}$;
* $\sin\theta<0\iff\theta\in(-\pi,0)$.

These are the standard sign patterns of the circular functions restricted to $(-\pi,\pi]$: $\cos$ is strictly positive on $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$, vanishes exactly at the odd integer multiples of $\frac\pi2$, and is strictly negative on $\left(\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}2\right)$ — hence on $\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right]$, and, since $\cos$ is even, also on $\left(-\pi,-\frac\pi2\right)$. Likewise $\sin$ is strictly positive on $(0,\pi)$, vanishes exactly at the integer multiples of $\pi$, and, being odd, is strictly negative on $(-\pi,0)$. Note in particular that the three $\cos$-conditions (and separately the three $\sin$-conditions) partition $(-\pi,\pi]$, so each biconditional follows from the corresponding forward implications.

**(T) Tangent and arctangent.** Where $\cos\theta\ne0$ one defines $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}$. The restriction of $\tan$ to $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ is a strictly increasing bijection onto $\mathbb R$, and $\arctan\colon\mathbb R\to\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ is its inverse; in particular
$$\arctan(\tan\varphi)=\varphi\qquad\text{for all }\varphi\in\left(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2\right). \tag{2}$$

**(P) Periodicity of $\tan$.** For every real $\varphi$ with $\cos\varphi\ne0$,
$$\tan(\varphi\pm\pi)=\tan\varphi .$$
Indeed, $\cos(\varphi\pm\pi)=-\cos\varphi\ne 0$ (so the left side is defined) and $\sin(\varphi\pm\pi)=-\sin\varphi$, whence
$\tan(\varphi\pm\pi)=\dfrac{-\sin\varphi}{-\cos\varphi}=\dfrac{\sin\varphi}{\cos\varphi}=\tan\varphi$.

**(3) Sign transfer.** Since $r>0$, equation (1) gives that $\cos\theta$ has the same sign (positive, zero, or negative) as $x$, and $\sin\theta$ has the same sign as $y$.

**(4) The tangent of $\theta$.** If moreover $x\ne0$, then $\cos\theta=x/r\ne 0$, so $\tan\theta$ is defined and
$$\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}=\frac{y/r}{x/r}=\frac yx .$$

## Proof

Throughout Cases 1–5, $\mathbf a=x\mathbf i+y\mathbf j\ne\mathbf 0$, $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}>0$, and $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ is the unique angle satisfying (1), as guaranteed by (E).

### Case 1: $x>0$

By (3), $\cos\theta=x/r>0$, so by (S) we have $\theta\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$. Since $x\ne 0$, (4) gives $\tan\theta=y/x$. Applying $\arctan$ to both sides and using (2) with $\varphi=\theta$ — legitimate precisely because $\theta\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$ — we obtain
$$\arctan\frac yx=\arctan(\tan\theta)=\theta .$$
Hence $\theta=\arctan\dfrac yx$, as claimed.

### Case 2: $x<0$ and $y\ge 0$

By (3), $\cos\theta=x/r<0$ and $\sin\theta=y/r\ge0$. By (S), $\cos\theta<0$ gives
$$\theta\in\left(-\pi,-\tfrac\pi2\right)\cup\left(\tfrac\pi2,\pi\right],$$
while $\sin\theta\ge0$ gives $\theta\in(0,\pi)\cup\{0,\pi\}=[0,\pi]$. Intersecting the two,
$$\theta\in\left(\tfrac\pi2,\pi\right],\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac\pi2<\theta\le\pi .$$
Put $\varphi:=\theta-\pi$. Then $-\frac\pi2<\varphi\le 0$, and in particular $\varphi\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$. Since $\cos\theta\ne0$, (P) applies and, together with (4),
$$\tan\varphi=\tan(\theta-\pi)=\tan\theta=\frac yx .$$
Applying $\arctan$ and using (2):
$$\arctan\frac yx=\arctan(\tan\varphi)=\varphi=\theta-\pi ,$$
so $\theta=\arctan\dfrac yx+\pi$, as claimed.

(Check of the boundary subcase: if $y=0$ and $x<0$ the formula gives $\theta=\arctan 0+\pi=\pi$, which is indeed the direction of a vector pointing along the negative $x$-axis, and $\pi\in(-\pi,\pi]$.)

### Case 3: $x<0$ and $y<0$

By (3), $\cos\theta<0$ and $\sin\theta<0$. By (S), $\sin\theta<0$ gives $\theta\in(-\pi,0)$, and $\cos\theta<0$ gives $\theta\in\left(-\pi,-\frac\pi2\right)\cup\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right]$. Intersecting,
$$\theta\in\left(-\pi,-\tfrac\pi2\right),\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad -\pi<\theta<-\frac\pi2 .$$
Put $\varphi:=\theta+\pi$. Then $0<\varphi<\frac\pi2$, so $\varphi\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$. Since $\cos\theta\ne0$, (P) and (4) give
$$\tan\varphi=\tan(\theta+\pi)=\tan\theta=\frac yx ,$$
and applying $\arctan$ with (2),
$$\arctan\frac yx=\arctan(\tan\varphi)=\varphi=\theta+\pi ,$$
so $\theta=\arctan\dfrac yx-\pi$, as claimed.

### Case 4: $x=0$ and $y>0$

Here $r=\sqrt{0+y^2}=\lvert y\rvert=y>0$, so (1) reads $\cos\theta=0/y=0$ and $\sin\theta=y/y=1$. By (S), $\cos\theta=0$ with $\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]$ forces $\theta\in\left\{-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right\}$. Since $\sin\left(-\frac\pi2\right)=-1\ne1$ and $\sin\frac\pi2=1$, the second condition selects
$$\theta=\frac\pi2 .$$

### Case 5: $x=0$ and $y<0$

Here $r=\lvert y\rvert=-y>0$, so $\cos\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=y/(-y)=-1$. As in Case 4, $\cos\theta=0$ forces $\theta\in\left\{-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right\}$, and only $\theta=-\frac\pi2$ has $\sin\theta=-1$. Hence
$$\theta=-\frac\pi2 .$$

### Case 6: $x=0$ and $y=0$

Then $\mathbf a=\mathbf 0$ and $r=0$. The defining relation $\mathbf a=r(\cos\theta\,\mathbf i+\sin\theta\,\mathbf j)$ is satisfied by *every* real $\theta$, since the right-hand side equals $\mathbf 0$ for all $\theta$; equivalently, the normalised components $x/r$, $y/r$ of (1) are not defined. Thus no angle is singled out, and, per (D), the zero vector has no direction: $\theta$ is undefined. This is the sixth line of the statement.

### Conclusion

The six cases
$$x>0;\quad x<0,\ y\ge0;\quad x<0,\ y<0;\quad x=0,\ y>0;\quad x=0,\ y<0;\quad x=0,\ y=0$$
are pairwise disjoint and together exhaust $\mathbb R^2$: the first three cover $x\ne0$ (splitting on $\operatorname{sign} x$, and for $x<0$ on the sign of $y$), and the last three cover $x=0$ (splitting on the sign of $y$). In each case the value of $\theta$ has been determined and agrees with the displayed formula. $\blacksquare$

## Remarks

1. In Cases 1–3 the quotient $y/x$ is defined precisely because $x\ne0$; in Cases 4–6 no arctangent expression is used, which is necessary, since there $y/x$ is meaningless.

2. The formula never returns a value outside $(-\pi,\pi]$. Indeed $\arctan$ takes values in $\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$, so: Case 1 yields $\theta\in\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)$; Case 2 yields $\theta\in\left(\frac\pi2,\frac{3\pi}2\right)$ a priori, but the sharper bound $\theta\le\pi$ proved above (from $\sin\theta\ge0$) confines it to $\left(\frac\pi2,\pi\right]$; Case 3 yields $\theta\in\left(-\frac{3\pi}2,-\frac\pi2\right)$ a priori and, by the argument above, in fact $\theta\in\left(-\pi,-\frac\pi2\right)$. Thus the endpoint $\pi$ is attained (Case 2 with $y=0$) while $-\pi$ is not, exactly matching the half-open convention $(-\pi,\pi]$.

3. The split on the sign of $y$ when $x<0$ is essential and cannot be replaced by a split on the sign of the quotient $y/x$ (equivalently, on the sign of $\arctan(y/x)$). The quotient $y/x$ is unchanged under $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$, so it cannot distinguish a vector from its negative; any rule of the form "$\theta=\arctan(y/x)$ if $y/x>0$, $\theta=\arctan(y/x)+\pi$ if $y/x<0$" therefore misassigns the direction on a full quadrant's worth of vectors. For instance, $\mathbf a=\mathbf i-\mathbf j$ has $y/x=-1<0$ and such a rule would return $\frac{3\pi}4$, whereas the true direction is $-\frac\pi4$ (here $x=1>0$, and Case 1 correctly gives $\theta=\arctan(-1)=-\frac\pi4$). Similarly, adding $+\pi$ uniformly whenever $x<0$ would push Case 3 out of $(-\pi,\pi]$, into $\left(\pi,\frac{3\pi}2\right)$; subtracting $\pi$ there is precisely the renormalisation back into the required interval, and it changes the angle by a full $2\pi$ relative to the $+\pi$ convention, hence names the same direction.

4. Equivalently, the six cases together define the two-argument arctangent $\theta=\operatorname{atan2}(y,x)$ on $\mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$.
